## 1. Identification Strategy  

Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered treatment adoption, complemented by an event-study specification.  

•  Why DID?  
– E-ZPass is introduced at different toll plazas in different months (1998-2001).  
– “Near” mothers experience a sharp decline in localized traffic-related pollution exactly at adoption; “far” mothers in the same labor-housing market do not.  
– The set-up naturally produces two dimensions of variation: space (near vs. far) and time (pre vs. post).  

•  Why event study?  
– To display dynamic effects, test for pre-trends, and quantify how quickly birth outcomes respond.  

•  Alternative methods (IV, RDD) are less attractive: IV would need a first stage linking E-ZPass to pollution at monitors, then pollution to births—less precise; RDD (distance to plaza) would not exploit the time shock and would force comparison of different neighborhoods.  

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
TREAT_it = 1 if mother i lives within 2 km of her nearest toll plaza in calendar quarter t **and** that plaza has already adopted E-ZPass by conception month; 0 otherwise.  
(Conception ≈ birth date – gestational age.)  

Control group  
Mothers living 2–10 km from the same plaza in the same quarter; they share macro environment but essentially no exposure to toll-booth idling emissions. (We will show robustness to 2–5 km and 5–10 km rings.)  

Treatment timing / event date  
τ_p = month in which plaza p activated E-ZPass (obtained from Turnpike Authority records).  
Each birth is assigned the τ_p of the plaza closest to the mother.  

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: Absent E-ZPass, infant health for near-plaza births would have trended like that for farther-away births.  
Plausibility: Both sets of mothers live in the same towns/ZIPs and face the same state-level shocks. We can examine pre-trends in an event study and include ZIP×year FE.  

A2. No contemporaneous shocks differentially hitting the near ring precisely at τ_p (e.g., opening of a factory, new obstetric clinic).  
Plausibility: Toll-plaza footprint did not change; adoption typically occurred overnight with no construction. We will include plaza×time-varying traffic controls and show robustness to adding block-group time trends.  

A3. No selective migration tied to the timing of E-ZPass (no “sorting on treatment”).  
Plausibility: The switch was unannounced to the public until days before activation and had no obvious housing market salience. We will verify that mother characteristics (age, education, race) are stable around τ_p.  

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): Pollution decline at plaza p does not affect mothers more than 10 km away nor increase traffic elsewhere in a way that biases the ring comparison.  
Plausibility: Traffic volumes change little; idling time falls only locally. We can show pollution monitors 5–15 km away record no significant change.  

## 4. Main Threats and Mitigations  

Threat 1: Differential pre-trends.  
Mitigation: Event-study coefficients for leads should be flat; include mother ZIP×year FE; placebo E-ZPass dates one year earlier.  

Threat 2: Residential sorting / compositional change.  
Mitigation: Check whether the distribution of maternal covariates changes discontinuously at adoption; re-estimate controlling flexibly for these covariates; restrict to mothers who lived in the same census block one year earlier (subset available from linkage of births to prior DMV records).  

Threat 3: Spillovers to the control ring (pollution may decline 2–10 km away).  
Mitigation: Use alternative control radii (10–20 km), and estimate dose-response using distance bands × post; validate using EPA monitors at multiple radii.  

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dim fixed effects
library(did)           # Callaway & Sant’Anna staggered DID
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Data Loading -----------------------------------------------------------
births  <- read_csv("birth_records_1997_2002.csv")      # one row per infant
plazas  <- read_csv("toll_plaza_locations_dates.csv")   # id, lat, lon, ezpass_date
monitors<- read_csv("pollution_monitors.csv")

# 2. Merge geospatial info --------------------------------------------------
# Already geocoded: births has lat, lon of mother's address
# Compute distance (km) to nearest toll plaza
plaza_coords <- plazas %>% select(plaza_id, pl_lat = lat, pl_lon = lon)

births <- births %>% 
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(
    nearest_plaza = plaza_coords$plaza_id[
      which.min( geosphere::distHaversine(c(lon, lat),
                                          plaza_coords %>% select(pl_lon, pl_lat)) )
    ],
    dist_km = min( geosphere::distHaversine(c(lon, lat),
                                            plaza_coords %>% select(pl_lon, pl_lat)) )/1000
  ) %>% ungroup()

births <- births %>% 
  left_join(plazas %>% select(plaza_id, ez_date), by = c("nearest_plaza" = "plaza_id"))

# conception month = birth_date - gestational_age_weeks * 7
births <- births %>% 
  mutate(conception_date = as.Date(birth_date) - gest_age_weeks*7,
         treat       = (dist_km <= 2 & conception_date >= ez_date),
         post        = if_else(conception_date >= ez_date, 1, 0),
         near        = if_else(dist_km <= 2, 1, 0),
         ring2_10    = dist_km > 2 & dist_km <= 10,
         year_q      = paste0(year(conception_date), "Q", quarter(conception_date)),
         plaza_fe    = as.factor(nearest_plaza)
  )

# 3. Main DID regression ----------------------------------------------------
# Outcome: birth weight in grams
did_bw <- feols(birth_weight ~ treat | plaza_fe + year_q, 
                data = births %>% filter(dist_km <= 10),
                cluster = ~nearest_plaza)

summary(did_bw)

# 4. Event Study using staggered adoption ----------------------------------
# Relative month to plaza activation
births <- births %>% 
  mutate(rel_month = interval(ez_date, conception_date) %/% months(1)) # negative = lead

es <- feols(birth_weight ~ i(rel_month, near, ref = -1) | plaza_fe + year_q,
            data = births %>% filter(dist_km <= 10 & abs(rel_month) <= 36),
            cluster = ~nearest_plaza)

iplot(es)   # pre-trend graph

# 5. Robustness: placebo adoption one year earlier -------------------------
births <- births %>% 
  mutate(fake_ez = ez_date - years(1),
         placebo  = (dist_km <= 2 & conception_date >= fake_ez))

placebo_bw <- feols(birth_weight ~ placebo | plaza_fe + year_q,
                    data = births %>% filter(dist_km <= 10),
                    cluster = ~nearest_plaza)

summary(placebo_bw)
```

## 6. Expected Results  

Prediction: Removing toll-booth congestion reduces maternal exposure to CO/NOx/PM, improving fetal growth. I expect:  
– Birth weight +25 – 40 g (≈ 0.06 σ) for babies whose mothers lived within 2 km.  
– 8–10 percent decline in low-birth-weight incidence.  
– Gestational age increase of 0.1 weeks; 5 percent decline in prematurity.  

Magnitude rationale: Prior literature links a 1 ppm drop in CO or 10 µg/m³ drop in PM2.5 during pregnancy to ~10–20 g higher birth weight. EPA monitor data suggest ≥2 ppm CO and 5–8 µg/m³ PM2.5 declines right at plazas.  

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1  Parallel trends visually supported (event-study leads) ............... 1  
C2  No differential composition changes .................................. 1  
C3  No anticipation of treatment (surprise switch-on) .................... 1  
C4  No other policy shocks coinciding with treatment locally ............. 0.5  
C5  No spillovers/contamination of control group ........................ 0.5  
Total (out of 5) ........................................................ 4.0  

Overall, the design should credibly isolate the causal impact of congestion-driven pollution on infant health.
